19652-a-ball-player-s-career-being-the-p:
Marshalltown, Iowa, opens this baseball memoir, praised as a handsome town of some thirteen thousand people. A Ball Player's Career presents itself as the personal experiences and recollections of its player-author. Books of this kind came from the first stars of professional baseball. They let fans hear the game described by a man who played it.

Readers get the early pro game from inside: travel, pay, crowds, and clubhouse life. Such memoirs helped turn ballplayers into national figures. They also fixed stories that later histories would test. The value here is the first-hand voice from baseball's rough early decades. Few records of that era feel this direct.
19734-the-fairy-book-the-best-popular-st:
The Fairy Book promises the best popular fairy stories, selected and rendered anew. Its preface speaks plainly to parents and children. In real life, it warns, beautiful people are not always good. Ugly people are not always wicked either. Elder sisters are not all ungenerous, nor stepmothers all cruel. Tender young hearts, it says, are reached by fancy as soon as by reason.

Retellings shaped how generations first met fairy tales. Editors softened some cruelties and kept the wonders. A preface like this one argues for the tales' honesty. It defends fancy as a teacher in its own right. The stories inside are the shared stock of childhood. This book shows Victorians handing that stock down, carefully.
19908-essays-on-scandinavian-literature:
Hjalmar Hjorth Boyesen published Essays on Scandinavian Literature in 1895. His Henrik Ibsen chapter, he explains, grew into its own book. That three-hundred-page study appeared the year before. It must be read as supplementary to this volume. His Björnson chapter nearly suffered the same expansion. Only heroic condensation kept it inside these covers. Boyesen, a Norwegian immigrant, interpreted the North for America.

Boyesen taught literature at Columbia and wrote novels too. He knew Ibsen's Norway from inside its culture. These essays carry Scandinavian writing to English readers early. Ibsen, Björnson, and their peers get full, serious treatment. The book marks America's discovery of modern Northern letters. Its enthusiasm still instructs and persuades.
19914-arabic-authors-a-manual-of-arabian:
Arabic Authors is a manual of Arabian history and literature by F. F. Arbuthnot. It hopes for a day when Oriental languages fill leisure hours. So much is to be learnt from Oriental literature, the author argues. King's College, London, is praised as full of promise for such study. A future generation thirsting for knowledge might study Arabic as a pastime. The manual itself opens that door for English readers.

Arbuthnot translated and promoted Eastern literature in Victorian Britain. His manual surveys poets, historians, and storytellers of Arabia. Short lives and work-lists guide beginners through centuries. The Thousand and One Nights looms over such surveys. This one stays practical, a handbook rather than a romance. It shows Oriental studies entering general culture.
19998-rural-architecture:
Lewis F. Allen wrote Rural Architecture to improve American farm buildings. Friends solicited the book, Allen says, believing he could help landholders. Without their urging, these pages would probably never have appeared. Practical farmers are his declared audience throughout. Plans for farmhouses, barns, and outbuildings fill the volume. Allen was a noted New York stock breeder and agricultural editor.

Farm architecture was a reform cause in the 1850s. Bad barns wasted stock, feed, and labor visibly. Allen gives designs, costs, and siting advice in full. His own farming success backed the authority claimed. The book belongs with Downing's country-house movement. It shows the model farm becoming an American ideal.
20101-under-fire:
Under Fire is a tale of soldiers, home, and the pride of a plains family. A soldier son comes home with an honored name in his trade. His parents glow with pride to have him under their roof again. Two sturdy, plains-bred little Cranstons add noise and joy to the house.

War still hangs over such a homecoming in the tale. Health, fame, and family love meet the strain of service life. The book shows how frontier homes bore the costs of war. Readers get a warm, tense story of return after danger and long absence.
20131-the-mask-a-story-of-love-and-adven:
Arthur Hornblow published The Mask in 1913, a story of love and adventure. News breaks of a huge gem found after blasting at some rocks. The land sits next to tracts of the Americo-African Mining Company. Some say the firm is already buying the ground for itself.

If true, the giant stone means a windfall for its Yankee owners. Diamonds, deals, and desire drive a tale set around African mines. The mask of the title hints at hidden faces and false shows. Readers get romance and risk in the world of gems and gold.
20406-epic-and-romance-essays-on-medieva:
W. P. Ker, a leading scholar of old literature, wrote Epic and Romance to explain the great stories of medieval Europe. The essays treat heroic poems, sagas, and romances as serious art. Ker writes for readers who want the old tales understood, not merely retold.

One essay wrestles with the Icelandic historian Sturla and the rivalry of a king and his father-in-law, Duke Skule. Ker praises the work of his friend Dr. Björn Magnússon Olsen on these hard problems. The book remains a guide to how epic strength and romance wonder grew side by side.
20572-marie-claire:
Marie-Claire is Marguerite Audoux's novel of a French orphan girl, drawn from the writer's own hard childhood. Marie-Claire grows up in a convent orphanage and goes out to work on farms and in service. The telling is plain, close, and quietly heartbreaking.

She remembers her sister's torments in their childhood games. The girl used to collect earthworms and hold them up close to her face. When she claimed she was no longer in pain, their keeper sent them both outdoors. One day her sister threw a handful of earthworms onto her dress. Such small cruelties mark the book's truthful eye.
20631-chosen-peoples-being-the-first-art:
Chosen Peoples, published in 1919, was the first Arthur Davis Memorial Lecture, delivered by Israel Zangwill. Zangwill, the Anglo-Jewish novelist, took up the hard idea of the chosen people. He spoke just after a war that had shown where racial pride could lead.

The recent show of racial arrogance in Germany, he notes, has handed the Allies a new weapon. An American writer in the Bookman declared that Germanism is Judaism. The proposition, Zangwill warns, contains just that dash of truth which is more dangerous than a falsehood. The lecture untangles that dash with care.
20657-tales-from-shakespeare:
Charles and Mary Lamb wrote Tales from Shakespeare to retell the plays as stories for young readers. Charles took the tragedies and Mary the comedies, in retellings first published in 1807. Their versions brought Shakespeare into the nursery without flattening his plots.

The Tempest opens the book. There was once an old man whose name was Prospero, and his daughter Miranda, a very beautiful young lady. She came to the island so young that she had no memory of any human face but her father's. The Lambs' plain, warm style has carried readers into Shakespeare for two centuries.
20702-a-general-plan-for-a-mail-communic:
A General Plan for a Mail Communication by Steam proposes regular steam packet routes to carry Britain's mail overseas. When sails ruled, letters waited on wind and season. The plan argues that steam can give the mail fixed days and faster passages between Great Britain and its distant ports.

It leans on expert proof. Mr. Napier of Glasgow, called an able and practical engineer, told the Post Office Commissioners in 1836 what steamers could do. Boats of 240 horsepower and 620 tons, he said, could be furnished at known prices. Such pamphlets helped push Britain into the steam age of world mail.
20733-critical-miscellanies-vol-1-of-3-e:
Robespierre and the close of the Reign of Terror open the first essay in Critical Miscellanies. The writer takes up a new French book on the fall of Robespierre. Those events bear the calendar name of Thermidor, in Year Two of the French Republic.

Victorian essay craft is on full show here, with long views of men and ideas. The piece weighs how a revolution turned on its own leaders. Later essays in the set treat other great figures and books. Readers who like bold, old-style literary essays will find strong opinions, wide reading, and prose built for argument rather than speed.
20740-myths-and-legends-of-all-nations-f:
Prometheus and Epimetheus, Forethought and Afterthought, open Myths and Legends of All Nations. The two brothers were sons of Titans who fought Jupiter and were chained below. Yet the brothers, for some reason, escaped that harsh fate.

Famed tales from Greece and other lands fill the book, retold in clear prose for general readers. Gods, heroes, gifts of fire, and hard lessons follow one after another. Such sets once served as a first door into world myth for many homes. The simple retelling keeps the old plots clear while trimming the hard parts of the source tales.
20784-eighth-annual-report-of-the-bureau:
Pueblo building in Tusayan and Cibola leads the eighth annual report of the Bureau of Ethnology. Victor Mindeleff studied those towns of stone and adobe in close detail. James Stevenson adds a study of a Navajo rite and its mythic sand painting.

Staff work by Cosmos Mindeleff, Garrick Mallery, James Mooney, and Jeremiah Curtin fills the report. The bureau sent trained men to record native life before it changed. Their plates and plans keep much that would else be lost. This 1886-87 volume is a rich trove for students of the native Southwest and its old towns.
20902-the-clyde-mystery-a-study-in-forge:
Plates from Gillen, learned boards, and Scots societies crowd the thanks in The Clyde Mystery. Andrew Lang turns to finds claimed as relics near the Clyde. Forgery and folklore, his subtitle warns, both haunt the case at hand.

Lang, a famed folklorist, tests stones and tales said to prove old Scots glory. He weighs proof with wit, lore, and a sceptic's sharp eye. The Clyde finds had stirred pride and doubt in learned Scotland. His study shows how scholars sort true relics from fond fakes, a craft as gripping as the finds themselves when told by Lang.
20953-by-the-christmas-fire:
Turning a sword to a pruning hook takes a smith, but a bayonet to a poker takes none. Samuel McChord Crothers opens By the Christmas Fire, from 1908, on that fireside thought. Severed from its rifle, the blade's new work is to coax winter flames.

Crothers, a beloved essayist and preacher, gathers warm talks for the Christmas season. Home, giving, faith, and good humour glow through his gentle pages. His essays were famed for kindness lit by quiet wit. This book suits slow winter reading, each piece a small fire of its own against the cold and dark outside.
21053-an-anthology-of-german-literature:
Sixty-nine lines of alliterative verse are all that survive of Germany's oldest heroic song, Calvin Thomas notes. The Kassel manuscript of the eighth or ninth century keeps that fragment safe. Its tongue mixes Low and High German, with gaps and doubtful words.

Thomas's anthology of German literature spans that fragment to near his own day of 1906. Poems, plays, tales, and essays appear in English versions with learned notes. He built the book for American students new to German letters. It maps a vast literature in one volume, from heroic lays to Goethe and beyond, with a teacher's steady hand.
21090-brief-history-of-english-and-ameri:
Henry A. Beers combined his outline sketches of English and American literature into this single brief history. It was published in New York, with copyrights running from 1886 to 1897. John Fletcher Hurst added an introduction and extra chapters on religious and theological writing in both countries. The book was aimed at students and general readers.

Beers moves through the main writers and periods of two literatures in a compact survey. Hurst argues that preachers and students of religion alike need real knowledge of literature. Indexes and page markers help readers use it as a reference. It shows how the two literatures were taught side by side in its day.
21098-the-independence-of-claire:
Claire Gifford has lived for three years in a Brussels pension when Mrs George de Horne Vaizey's novel opens. She stands in the salon asking herself one question: can she marry the man proposed for her? Her brain says she must, out of duty to her family, while her heart rebels.

Vaizey writes about young, well-brought-up women of Edwardian times, their money worries, clothes, parties, and marriage choices. Claire seems headed for a big mistake before matters sort themselves out. The title points to her real struggle, which is less about one suitor than about standing on her own feet and choosing her own life.
21214-the-law-and-lawyers-of-pickwick-a-:
Frank Lockwood, a Queen's Counsel and Member of Parliament, delivered this lecture in York and then in London in December 1893. Its subject is the law and lawyers of Dickens's Pickwick Papers. Lord Russell of Killowen, then Attorney General, introduced him at Morley Hall in Hackney. The Roxburghe Press printed the lecture in 1894.

Lockwood, himself a witty advocate, examines Sergeant Buzfuz and the famous trial of Bardell against Pickwick. That breach of promise case turns on chops, tomata sauce, and comic cross talk. He explains the real law behind Dickens's fun. An original drawing of Buzfuz fronts the little book.
21303-devon-boys-a-tale-of-the-north-sho:
Three boarders at Barnstaple Grammar School spend their summer holiday on Devon's north shore in George Manville Fenn's tale, set in 1752. Bob Chowne is a doctor's cross-grained son, and Bigley Uggleston is a fisherman's pleasant boy. Sep Duncan, the narrator, is a naval officer's son whose father has just bought a stretch of cliffs.

The boys blast a rock from the cliff top and uncover a rich vein of galena, lead and silver ore. Sep's father opens a mine on the spot. Escapades follow: rescues at sea by a French smuggler and a French attack aimed at twenty boxes of silver bullion stored from the mine.
21390-the-golden-grasshopper-a-story-of-:
Ernst Verner, a Dutch boy, tells his own tale in W. H. G. Kingston's The Golden Grasshopper. His parents died in Holland for their Protestant faith, and he reaches an England split by creed. Between King Edward, Queen Mary, and Queen Elizabeth, belief could cost a life.

The story first came out in 1870 as The Royal Merchant, in the days of Sir Thomas Gresham. Gresham, the great London merchant, stands at the heart of the tale's world of trade. Boys on the run, a hostile priest, and slow Channel crossings add the peril. Kingston revised the book near the end of his life.
21404-from-powder-monkey-to-admiral-a-st:
Three boys join the navy at its lowest rung in W. H. G. Kingston's From Powder Monkey to Admiral. Kingston wrote the story for the Boys' Own Paper when that paper first started. His aim was to show how a plain lad might climb to the top rank.

Powder monkeys ran powder to the guns in battle, small targets who often lived through fights. Real men like Benbow and Hopson had made just that climb before. The three boys share the usual run of Kingston sea adventures. Only one of them, though, wins his way to the quarterdeck and a midshipman's place.
21724-the-handbook-of-soap-manufacture:
Two chemists, W. H. Simmons and H. A. Appleton, wrote this practical handbook of soap making, published in London in 1908. The opening chapter defines soap and explains how it cleans, through the splitting of fats by water and alkali. Later chapters take up the make-up of oils and fats and how they turn into soap.

The authors cover old research, modern methods, and the tools and tests a working soap maker needs. Twenty-seven pictures help show plant and process. The book was made for the trade, not the home kitchen. It gives a clear snapshot of factory soap making at the start of the twentieth century, chemistry and craft side by side.
21908-chums-of-the-camp-fire:
Bullfrog hunting opens Chums of the Camp Fire, a 1915 boys' book by Lawrence J. Leslie. Steve, Toby, and Max count thirteen frog saddles and aim for twenty before they quit. Toby stammers his tallies while the boys dream of the Dismal Swamp, where a bushel basket might be filled. The chapters roll into the woods: a terrible roar, a mysterious ham thrower, and a wild animal trap.

A strange disappearance and a plot against the missing link raise the stakes before the last camp fire. Leslie writes in the brisk series style, each chapter a small adventure with a hook. The frontispiece shows Max sure they can capture the monkey. It is cheerful outdoor fiction for boys of the camping age, all appetite and schemes.
21957-the-psychology-of-singing-a-ration:
Singing teachers are put on trial in David C. Taylor's The Psychology of Singing, first published in 1908 and reprinted in 1922. Taylor calls his book a rational method of voice culture built on a study of all systems, ancient and modern. In no art, he says, do art and nature seem so one as in singing. A perfect voice hides its own art completely.

Part one surveys modern instruction: breathing, registers, resonance. Part two attacks its fallacies one by one, from breath control to nasal resonance and mechanical management of the voice. Part three seeks the basis of a real science of voice. Taylor writes as a reformer with a laboratory mind. The book remains a sharp, readable argument that singing is guided by the ear and mind, not by throat tricks.
22071-marjorie-dean-college-sophomore:
Pauline Lester sent her heroine back to Sanford College in Marjorie Dean, College Sophomore, published in 1922. Marjorie and her friends return for their second year full of plans. Jerry speaks for them all: whose fault is it, she retorts, that she and Muriel have lost last year's trusting faith in reception committees? As freshmen they stood on the station platform like dummies, with no one to bid them the time of day.

The slight rankles, and the Sans Soucians, the campus society at the books' centre, must mend its ways. Lester's Marjorie Dean books followed their heroine through high school and college. This sophomore volume mixes friendship, snobbery, and reform in the series' earnest style.
22211-gilian-the-dreamer-his-fancy-his-l:
Neil Munro, the Scottish novelist of John Splendid, published Gilian the Dreamer in 1899. His subtitle promises Gilian's fancy, his love, and adventure. The book opens by a Highland river as rain beats on plane and beech leaves. The scent of the blossoming gean-tree hangs sweet and haunting round the road.

Gilian is a dreamer in a hard, practical world of Highland trade and kirk. Munro follows his fancies, his love, and his brushes with rougher men. Mist, hills, and old woods colour every chapter, as the opening sigh of wind suggests. The novel is a tender, melancholy piece of the Scottish literary revival.
22218-the-street-that-wasn-t-there:
Clifford D. Simak and Carl Jacobi wrote The Street That Wasn't There for Comet magazine in July 1941. Mr. Jonathon Chambers leaves his house on Maple Street and finds the world subtly wrong. Chambers was once a professor whose book cost him his university post in a scandal. What he taught has been forgotten, but it was revolutionary enough to ruin him.

Now the forgotten theory seems to be coming true around him. Streets, neighbours, and his own past refuse to stay fixed. Simak and Jacobi build the unease quietly, in a small town at evening. The story is a neat early tale of reality slipping, by two masters of the pulp magazines.
22255-the-counts-of-gruye-re:
Mrs. Henry de la Pasture translated The Counts of Gruyère from the French history of the Swiss counts. The book opens on a green plain where the first steps of the Alps rise like an amphitheatre. A little castled city on a solitary hill has watched the scene for a thousand years. That city is Gruyères, and its counts ruled the valley for centuries.

The history follows the counts through crusades, wars, debts, and marriages. The last count, Michael, lost the county in the 1500s, and the castle passed to Fribourg and Bern. De la Pasture, herself a novelist, made the dry records readable. The volume is Swiss local history in its romantic vein.
22280-views-and-reviews-essays-in-apprec:
W. E. Henley, poet and editor, gathered his criticism in Views and Reviews: Essays in Appreciation in 1890. Henley was a formidable judge with a wooden leg and a thunderous taste. On Dickens he is deliciously severe by proxy: Andrew Lang, he notes, mocks those who cannot read Dickens, yet loves only the humourist. For Dickens the artist in drama and romance Lang has as little sympathy as the most practical reader.

Henley himself reads generously and judges sharply. Essays on novelists, poets, and dramatists fill the volume. His criticism is personal, quotable, and often unjust in an interesting way. The book is a monument of the 1890s literary battlefield, where reputations were made by fighting.
22281-the-facts-about-shakespeare:
William Allan Neilson of Harvard and Ashley Horace Thorndike of Columbia wrote The Facts about Shakespeare as a plain handbook. They begin with an England in motion. When Elizabeth came to the throne, England was still largely Catholic after nine centuries. When Shakespeare died, it was Protestant and turning Puritan, and religion, politics, literature, and commerce had all changed around him.

Against that moving background the professors set the documents: baptism, marriage, will, and the Stratford monument. They separate record from legend with scholarly care. The book was written for students who wanted the evidence without the fog. It remains a sober, useful life in brief, all facts and no Bardolatry.
22303-personality-in-literature:
Personality in Literature is a critical essay preserved from Project Gutenberg, with no author named in the record. It opens at an exhibition of Post-Impressionist pictures. The writer walks the show with an artist who helped create it.

Forced to speak in questions, the writer faces a canvas that looks formless and ugly to untrained eyes. That awkward scene sets up the larger topic named in the title. The essay asks how the maker's own character shows through in creative work. Readers get period criticism in a personal voice, caught between polite manners and honest doubt about new art.
22318-crocker-s-hole-from-slain-by-the-d:
Crocker's Hole is one of R. D. Blackmore's tales from Slain by the Doones. Where other Doone stories chase outlaws, this one slows down for water. Its quoted passage follows small streams with loving patience.

Tricklets slip through water-grass, make moss, and forget themselves in the ooze. Kettles are filled from the same small flows at cottage doors. One and all, Blackmore writes, they come to the same thing at last: the river. That gentle close shows his gift for West Country landscape. Readers get a quiet nature piece tucked inside a book of rougher tales.
22752-the-pirate-of-panama-a-tale-of-the:
William MacLeod Raine wrote The Pirate of Panama, a 1914 tale of the fight for buried treasure. Raine, a prolific western novelist, here trades the range for the sea roads of Panama, where tales of pirate gold still drew adventurers in the canal years. His subtitle promises the fight, and the book delivers it.

The opening is all weather and nerves: a chill wind swept the city and cut to the marrow. From a hilltop the narrator watches his car sliding down toward him as he clings to the curb, postponing the plunge into the flowing street. Modern streets give way to older, bloodier trails southward. Raine writes clean, fast adventure in his western manner, transplanted to treasure country.
22866-an-ounce-of-cure:
A doctor's warning opens An Ounce of Cure, a short story about health and denial. Fifty-five is a dangerous age, he tells his patient gravely. He asks about a cough, heartburn after dinner, and sleeping propped on pillows. Then comes the sigh. The man has gone ten years without a checkup.

The tale builds its tension from that ordinary neglect. Prevention, the old proverb promises, beats any cure, and the story tests the proverb on a man who would rather not know. Its setting is the modern clinic rather than the sickroom of older fiction. Readers get a compact, pointed piece of mid-century magazine storytelling, with a moral carried by scene and dialogue rather than lecture.
22996-the-rover-boys-on-snowshoe-island-:
Arthur M. Winfield races his Rover Boys across the ice in The Rover Boys on Snowshoe Island, published in 1918. On a Saturday in early winter, Colby Hall's cadets pack the smooth ice of the lake beside their school. Tag, hockey, and snapping the whip fill the hours until Gif Garrison, head of the athletic association, suggests a race.

Snowshoe Island and an old lumberman's treasure box wait beyond the schoolyard fun. Winfield, writing as the Rover Boys' chronicler, delivers the series formula, sport, mystery, and clean rivalry in equal parts. The cadet setting updates Tom, Dick, and Sam's world for a new generation. Millions of boys read these books, and this volume shows the machine working smoothly.
23014-a-soldier-of-the-empire:
Thomas Nelson Page guards a New Orleans quarter in A Soldier of the Empire. Neighbors came to treat the old Sergeant as the Quarter's true keeper of order. He preserved its quiet better than every gendarme ever posted inside its bounds. And thus the children all knew him.

An old soldier of Napoleon, settled in Louisiana, gives Page his figure of honor out of place and time. The empire fell, but its discipline keeps one neighborhood safe. Page tells the tale in his elegiac register, loyal to lost causes and the men who served them. Beneath the sentiment sits a shrewd portrait of authority earned by character. It is among his characteristic short works, compact and carefully warmed.
23044-the-merry-wives-of-windsor-the-wor:
Textual trouble heads The Merry Wives of Windsor in this Cambridge Shakespeare volume. The editors print the play's early text exactly as the 1602 quarto gives it, using Capell's preserved copy. They check that text against the second quarto of 1619 throughout.

That fuss exists because the Merry Wives survives in two very different early texts. The play inside is Shakespeare's sunniest piece of town comedy, Falstaff scheming after two merry wives who out-scheme him at every turn. Laundry baskets, jealous husbands, and a midnight fright at Herne's oak fill the plot. The edition lets readers enjoy the farce and inspect its foundations on the same page, a double pleasure this series made normal.
23141-the-island-treasure:
Captain Snaggs shouts orders in The Island Treasure. Captain Snaggs barks his orders in quick succession, hoarse words ringing fore and aft until the deck fittings seem to jingle. His drawl carries a strong nasal twang, as though half the speaking came through his nose.

A treasure island, a nasal captain, and a crew under full sail give this sea tale its classic furniture. George Manville Fenn, to whom the adventure is credited, stocked dozens of boys' books with just such gear. Storms, charts, and buried wealth turn the pages in order. The Snaggs portrait alone, all voice and authority, shows a practiced hand.
a-drama-on-the-seashore: A short Balzac tragedy set on the Breton coast: a father's guilt over a terrible crime, told against the sound of the sea. Somber and powerful in a few pages, it shows Balzac's gift for the stark and terrible. The Human Comedy's grimmest shoreline.
a-girl-of-high-adventure: A Girl of High Adventure, by Angela Brazil. The adventurous girl. This book preserves that story. The paper lived through the years. Later readers can locate it. It retains its place in time. Those who study the era will use it in their work.
a-history-of-english-literature: Robert Huntington Fletcher's history carries students from Beowulf to the moderns — Chaucer, Shakespeare, Milton, and all the great names. Clear, sound, and well-planned, it served generations of classrooms. A reliable guide to England's literary glory. His steady survey leads from Anglo-Saxon songs to the great Victorians with sure judgment.
a-journey-in-other-worlds-a-romance-of-t: John Jacob Astor's 1894 science fiction: a journey to Jupiter and Saturn in the year 2000. Written by America's richest man, it imagines a technocratic future. Fascinating early SF from an unlikely author. Astor died on the Titanic, giving his futurism a haunting frame.
a-study-in-tinguian-folk-lore: Fay-Cooper Cole's pioneering study records the folklore of the Tinguian people of the Philippines — their myths, rituals, and traditions gathered in the field. Early anthropology at its most dedicated and respectful. A precious record of a rich and distinctive culture.
adventure: Jack London's 1911 novel set on a Solomon Islands plantation, where the heroine Joan Lackland matches the men in courage and wits. Romance, disease, and labor troubles mix in a South Seas story unusually centered on a strong woman. London's Pacific fiction at its most vivid.
alice-sit-by-the-fire: J. M. Barrie's tender comedy follows Alice — a mother returning to children who barely remember her — through misunderstandings toward a loving reconciliation. The creator of Peter Pan shows his gentler, wistful side. A play of great charm and deep feeling.
along-the-shore: Rose Hawthorne Lathrop, Nathaniel's gifted daughter, gathers poems of the shore — sea moods, white sails, and the music of waves against rock. Her gentle lyrics carry a painter's eye for light on water and a daughter's inheritance of deep feeling. Quiet, graceful verse from a true minor poet.
at-aboukir-and-acre: At Aboukir and Acre, G, a, henty's napoleonic tale, the egyptian campaign. This book preserves that historical novel. The paper lasts as a quiet witness. Time has kept the file intact. The archive guards it with care.
at-the-earth-s-core: The book that launched Edgar Rice Burroughs's Pellucidar series: inventor Abner Perry's giant boring machine carries him and young David Innes down through the Earth's crust into a hollow world. Inside they find a savage land lit by a central sun, ruled by the cruel flying Mahars and their ape-like servants. Burroughs's inner-world adventure has thrilled readers for over a century.
beautiful-stories-from-shakespeare: E. Nesbit's 1907 retellings of Shakespeare's plays for children: twenty tales keeping the plots clear and the magic intact. The creator of the Bastable books brings her storytelling gift to the Bard. A wonderful first Shakespeare for young readers.
black-bartlemy-s-treasure: Black Bartlemy's Treasure, Jeffery Farnol's pirate adventure. The treasure hunt unfolds. This book preserves that tale. The archive keeps the paper open to all. Its pages add to the record of the past. Scholars prize such firsthand sources.
brandes-main-currents-in-19th-century-li:
Georg Brandes opens his landmark survey of European writing with The Emigrant Literature, here in English. Exiles driven out by revolt carried new ideas from land to land after the French Revolution. The Danish critic treats their books as sparks in a broad fire.

Brandes links life, politics, and art in one flowing account. He asks how writers in exile shaped the taste of a whole continent. Later volumes would take up France, Germany, and England in turn. This first book launched a six-volume work that changed how Europe read its own nineteenth century.
british-airships-past-present-and-future: George Whale's 1919 survey of Britain's airship program, from early experiments through the First World War. He traces the design of dirigibles, their wartime patrols against submarines, and dreams of peacetime air travel. Written just as the airship age peaked, it is a knowledgeable insider's record of a technology about to be eclipsed by the airplane.
castle-nowhere: Constance Fenimore Woolson sets this novel among the islands and shores of the Great Lakes, a region she knew intimately. Her characters — dreamers and wanderers drawn to the water — live out quiet dramas of love and loss against the vast inland seas. Woolson, a friend of Henry James, wrote with a subtlety that has won her lasting admirers.

Gregory Klimov, a Soviet officer who defected to the West, wrote The Terror Machine about the Soviet administration in occupied Germany after the Second World War. Klimov had served in that administration himself. Edward Crankshaw, a British Soviet expert, prefaced the English edition.

He describes arrests, deportations, informers, and the daily brutality of the occupation machine from inside its offices. The account is a defector's testimony, written in the early Cold War as warning and as evidence. Its detail is its value: names, offices, and methods, unvarnished. The book stands among the classic defector accounts that shaped the West's picture of the Soviet system.
govdocs-archive_org-NurembergAndTheOther:
A 1978 booklet from Historical Review Press, Nuremberg and the Other War Crimes Trials, surveys the International Military Tribunal of 1945 and 1946 and the trials that followed it. Historical Review Press was a revisionist publisher, and the booklet argues from that standpoint. It is a pamphlet of advocacy, not an official record.

It describes the scene at Nuremberg, the role of the OSS, and Justice Jackson's opening speech, then lists the defendants and sentences. Appendices take up Katyn, the bombing of civilians, and de-Nazification, pressing the charge that the trials were victors' justice. The booklet is a debated piece of revisionist literature, held complete for researchers of the argument.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-Crossfire_Cross: A publisher's flyer promotes Crossfire: The Plot That Killed Kennedy, Jim Marrs' book arguing that President Kennedy died in a plot. The same sheet carries an advertisement for a historical mystery by John Dickson Carr, issued in the same series. Flyers of this kind were trade publicity, printed to sell forthcoming books to shops and reviewers rather than to argue the case itself.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-Hosty-OswaldOne:
An FBI memorandum dated October 1, 1975 went from the Director to the Attorney General of the United States. It reports the Bureau's preliminary inquiry into an allegation concerning Lee Harvey Oswald. Twelve years after the assassination, a claim about Oswald still traveled the full height of the Justice Department.

A preliminary inquiry was the Bureau's first formal step, checking whether an allegation deserved a full investigation. That the Director himself signed off to the Attorney General shows the matter's sensitivity. The memo preserves the opening of that inquiry at the top of the department.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-SheridanSquareP: nsia-SheridanSquarePress Sheridan Square Press: the made public government document, captured as titled. Subject: government records. A bare file, kept as issued. An obscure item, complete. From the archive shelves, for readers of the files and readers.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_intellig:
In April 2018 President Donald Trump had nominated Gina Haspel to run the CIA, and the Archive posted her torture file. Declassified documents, it said, showed she personally supervised the torture of a detainee in 2002. That torture included at least three waterboarding sessions.

Haspel subsequently drafted the cable that ordered destruction of the videotapes of the torture. The posting also charged that she served as a senior official while the agency misled presidents, Congress, and the public about whether torture worked. The file assembled the public record against her at the moment the Senate weighed her nomination.
here-there-and-everywhere: Lord Frederic Hamilton, a British diplomat, soldier, and member of Parliament, fills this memoir with stories from a life spent across the empire. From African campaigns to London drawing rooms, he recalls the people and odd incidents he met along the way. Told with dry wit and no great reverence for rank, it is an insider's tour of the late Victorian world.
history-of-american-literature: Reuben Post Halleck's survey takes students from colonial beginnings through the flowering of American letters. Irving, Hawthorne, Emerson, Whitman, and Twain each receive their chapter in a narrative of how a new nation found its voice. Long used in American classrooms, the book offers a solid, readable map of the country's literary past.
hoadly-queries-recommended-to-the-author: Queries recommended to the authors of the late Discourse of free thinking, by Hoadly. The bishop's queries. This book preserves that pamphlet. Scholars prize such firsthand sources. The paper lived through the years. Time has kept the file intact through the years.
how-to-fail-in-literature-a-lecture: Andrew Lang's lecture on how to fail in literature: witty advice for aspiring authors. Ironic and delightful, it is the scholar at play. The funniest lecture on writing ever given. Lang's advice is better than most success manuals.
indian-why-stories-sparks-from-war-eagle: Frank Bird Linderman gathered these Native American "why" tales from storytellers of the Plains tribes. Around a lodge fire, elders explain how the coyote got his voice, why the bear has a short tail, and how the world came to be, in stories both funny and wise. Published in 1915, the book preserves oral traditions that were already fading, told with real warmth for the tellers.
kansas-women-in-literature:
Kansas Women in Literature is Nettie Garmer Barker's survey of women writers of Kansas. Its epigraphs boast that the state's children are a nobler pride than its walls of corn. Barker counts Kansas-born and adopted women alike in her galaxy of bright names. The first portrait treats Effie Graham, head of mathematics at Topeka High School.

Graham, Barker says, found romance in arithmetic and showed others the way in her lecture Living Arithmetic. Ex-Governor Hoch called her one of the most gifted women in a state noted for brilliant women. Graham lectured on moving into the king row, other people's children, and the larger service. Barker's sketches mix biography, praise, and quotation. The book preserves a state's pride in its women of letters.
kennedy-square:
Kennedy Square is a novel by F. Hopkinson Smith, set in a Southern square of the late fifties. Smith's preface quotes his own Fortunes of Oliver Horn for the square's portrait: magnolias, glossy box, and Noah's Ark church. Kennedy Square has no church, but it has an archdeacon's house instead. Its atmosphere, he promises, matches the older book's square.

Chapter one opens some sixty years earlier, in the square's great days. Smith builds his story on the square's families, their pride, their money troubles, and their honor. The Civil War era closes around them as the novel proceeds. Smith wrote of old Baltimore society with a painter's eye and a native's affection. Kennedy Square is his tribute to that vanishing world.
king-of-the-khyber-rifles-a-romance-of-a:
King of the Khyber Rifles: A Romance of Adventure is Talbot Mundy's 1916 novel of India's frontier, here in a combined edition. Its contents list eighteen chapters without titles. Captain Athelstan King of the Indian service is the hero. He works among the tribes of the Khyber Pass country, where Britain watched the road to Afghanistan.

The Khyber Rifles, the famous frontier regiment, give the book its name and setting. Mundy's tale mixes secret missions, tribal councils, and mountain fighting. A hidden valley and a mysterious woman stand at the center of the intrigue, by common report of the novel. Mundy knew India well and wrote its frontier with an insider's love of intrigue. The book made his name in adventure fiction.
kitty-trenire:
Mabel Quiller-Couch wrote Kitty Trenire, a story for young readers in twenty-one chapters. The opening chapters bring news, a drive, and storms at home and abroad. Kitty's family and friends fill the early scenes.

Later chapters bring Anna's arrival, lessons, alarms, and an exciting night. One chapter is called Missing, and another is called Banished. A girl named Betty has an escapade of her own. The book closes with a chapter titled Good in Everything, hinting at lessons learned through trouble. Home troubles matter as much as outdoor adventures here. Kitty must carry real duties while she is still quite young.
la-grenadiere:
Honoré de Balzac set his tale La Grenadière in a small house by the Loire. Ellen Marriage translated it into English. The house stands about a mile below the bridge of Tours.

Balzac describes white stone houses among gardens and vineyards along the cliffs. The finest fruit ripens there under a southern exposure. Generations of patient work cut terraces into the rock face. Against that calm, rich setting, he places a quiet story of a woman and her sons. Place matters deeply in this tale of a mother and sons. The calm house frames lives marked by loss and duty.
lady-baltimore:
Owen Wister, author of Western fiction, set his novel Lady Baltimore in the South. He dedicated it to S. Weir Mitchell with lifelong affection. A note to readers opens the book on a playful, serious theme.

Wister quotes Burns on seeing ourselves as others see us. He wishes artists could test their work as its audience first. That wish frames a story of manners and memory in an old Southern city. A young visitor meets a proud, fading society there. Romance and gentle comedy carry the clash of old and new ways.
lady-clare:
Alfred Tennyson's poem Lady Clare appears here with twenty-two illustrations. Six artists drew them, including Frederic Schell and F. S. Church. The pictures show lilies, a white doe, and the nurse Alice.

The ballad tells of a lady who seems high born and rich. Her nurse reveals a secret about her true birth. Clare must choose between rank and honest love. She gives up wealth rather than win her lover by a lie. Tennyson's short tale in verse remains a favorite for its clear moral and music. The nurse Alice drives the plot with one spoken truth. Clare's choice, once made, is held with quiet firmness.
landmarks-in-french-literature:
Lytton Strachey published Landmarks in French Literature in London in 1912. Seven chapters carry the reader from the Middle Ages to his own era. A list of authors and a bibliography close the book.

Strachey begins with origins, then treats the Renaissance. The age of Louis XIV gets its own chapter. He moves through the eighteenth century and the Romantic movement. A final chapter covers the age of criticism. His short survey became known for clear judgments and elegant prose about French writing. A chronology at the end helps students place each author. Strachey's brisk verdicts still spark argument among readers.
latin-literature:
J. W. Mackail wrote this survey of Latin literature for a series of manuals. The late Professor William Sellar had first agreed to write it. Mackail, his former pupil, finished the task after Sellar's death.

He offers the book as a tribute to his teacher and friend. Chapters begin with the Roman Republic and its early epic and tragedy. Comedy by Plautus and Terence follows. Mackail traces Roman writing from rough starts to classical polish. Students get a compact map of a vast literature in one volume. Mackail later became known as a critic and anthologist. His survey prizes style as much as bare literary fact.
lazarre:
Mary Hartwell Catherwood published her historical romance Lazarre in Indianapolis in 1901. The Bowen-Merrill Company issued it with illustrations by André Castaigne. One caption shows a figure mounting toward the guardians of an imperial court.

That court setting signals the tale's world of rank and intrigue. Catherwood built her reputation on romances set in earlier centuries. French and colonial history often supplied her scenes and characters. Lazarre belongs to that line of richly dressed historical fiction. Readers who enjoy court danger, loyalty, and lost identity will find her manner here.
lectures-on-dramatic-art-and-literature:
August Wilhelm von Schlegel's Lectures on Dramatic Art and Literature shaped Romantic criticism. The book opens with a warm defense of reading itself. A taste for reading, the motto says, shields a person against life's ills.

Schlegel surveys drama from the Greeks to his own century. He champions Shakespeare against French classical rules. His lectures helped Europe rethink what tragedy and comedy could be. Translators carried his ideas into English literary debate. The work remains a landmark of comparative literary history. German Romantic writers reshaped taste through these lectures. English poets and critics borrowed Schlegel's terms for decades.
letters-on-literature:
Andrew Lang's Letters on Literature collect his essays on books and writers. An introductory piece treats modern English poetry. Further letters treat Fielding, Longfellow, and a friend of Keats.

Virgil, Lucretius, and Plotinus represent the ancient world here. Aucassin and Nicolette brings in a medieval French tale. Richardson and Gérard de Nerval receive letters of their own. A dedication thanks a helpful friend Lang never met in person. The book shows Lang's wide, easy learning worn lightly. Lang also wrote on books for young American hunters, he jokes. His range runs from Homer to yesterday's poetry.
lister-s-great-adventure:
Harold Bindloss published this adventure novel in 1920. Part One, called Barbara's Rebellion, opens the contents. Cartwright meddles, and Barbara vanishes in early chapters. A girl on a platform and a trip to Winnipeg Beach follow.

Lister's dissatisfaction grows until a test confronts him. Part Two, The Reckoning, brings Vernon's plot into the open. Barbara returns, and Lister clears the ground for settlement. A dissatisfied shareholder and Cartwright's scruples complicate the ending. Shillito gets away and Barbara plays a part before the reckoning. Vernon's curiosity opens the plot threads of part one.
love-under-fire:
Love under Fire is a Civil War romance by Randall Parrish, dated 1911. Alonzo Kimball painted its five color pictures. The tale opens between the lines, with a despatch-bearer hunted down. A woman, Miss Willifred, soon holds the hero as her prisoner.

Chapters bring night adventures, an overheard talk, and a captured house. The villain Le Gaire forces decisions and fights a duel. The hero even becomes, for a time, a famous swordsman. Love and duty pull the young officer in opposite ways. Parrish writes brisk, old-fashioned war romance. It is full of rides, risks, and a brave heroine.
macleod-of-dare:
Macleod of Dare is a Scottish novel by William Black, printed at New York in 1883. Black had already won readers with A Princess of Thule. The first chapter names the six boys of Dare. It opens at sunset over the lonely western seas by Mull.

Ulva, Lunga, and the Dutchman's Cap darken on the water. In Castle Dare's great hall, candles blaze over a frugal supper. An old lady of proud, fine features sits at the table's head. Faithful Hamish serves the small company in the vast room. Black fills the tale with Highland scenery and sea air. His romance joins old clan pride to modern hearts.
measure-for-measure: William Shakespeare wrote Measure for Measure, and the record holds it under his name alone. The hosted sample for this entry preserves long notes by the head of Project Gutenberg. Those notes treat old spelling in Hamlet and in print shops of the time. No readable scene of Measure for Measure itself appears in the sample. This note stays with the title, the author, and that sample limit for that reason.
meyer-us4826581-controlled-process-for-t:
United States Patent 4,826,581, granted to Stanley A Meyer on May 2, 1989, covers a controlled process for making heat from gases, plus the gear to run it. The method patent is part of his eight-piece water fuel cell family. It widens his claims from engines to heat itself.

The process takes in his fuel gas, burns it under set controls, and draws off the heat for use. The filing spells out each stage, the burners, and the apparatus in claim language. Patents attest that a method was described as new, not that it works. Meyer's fuel claims were found fraudulent by an Ohio court in 1996.
miles-wallingford-sequel-to-afloat-and-a:
James Fenimore Cooper wrote this sea novel as the sequel to Afloat and Ashore. Miles Wallingford himself tells the story in the first person. The opening scene is a rescue: Miles has fought his rival Drewett in the water. Friends haul both men aboard the Wallingford and fight to revive the seemingly lifeless Drewett.

Below deck, Lucy Hardinge waits on her knees, praying for the news she fears. Cooper mixes sea action with the claims of love, honor, and old friendship. Miles narrates with hindsight, judging his younger self as he goes. The novel continues his double life between the merchant sea and home ashore.
monsieur-beaucaire:
Booth Tarkington's romance opens at the card table in Bath, England. The young Frenchman Beaucaire has guessed that a duke will cheat. He plucks the hidden card smilingly from the big Englishman's sleeve. Six silent men step from the entryway, and the duke stands caught, scarlet and white by turns.

Beaucaire promises not murder but disgrace, laughing his clear, light laugh. Behind his manners stands a mystery: Beaucaire is a French prince traveling in disguise, working as a barber. Nash, master of Bath society, dislikes the young Frenchman in the pump room. Tarkington's tale of wit, swordplay, and wooing became a beloved stage and screen romance.
my-buried-treasure:
Richard Harding Davis swears this tale of a treasure hunt is true. Only his partner's name is changed, to Edgar Powell. Powell led the trip and still makes flannels for a living. Davis says his own share is what the story earns.

The two had known each other at college, then lost touch. Powell came back with a plan and a buried hoard in mind. Davis tells what was said and done as best he can. No pact stops him from judging his friend in print. The result is crisp adventure writing, half confession and half yarn, from a master of the short tale.
mysticism-in-english-literature:
Caroline F. E. Spurgeon studies mysticism in great English writers here. Her note, dated April 1913, sets strict bounds at once. She treats only the type that seeks ultimate reality. American letters, though rich in such thought, are left out.

A line from Plato's Phaedo fronts the book on the few true mystics. Contents move from Plato and Plotinus to English thought. Love and beauty mystics include Shelley, Rossetti, and Browning. Keats and Coventry Patmore join that company. Spurgeon quotes Traherne, Jefferies, and Thompson with care. The book maps a quiet, deep stream in English writing.
myths-and-legends-of-our-own-land-volume:
Charles M. Skinner gives this whole volume to buried treasure and storied places. Captain Kidd stands first, the most widespread man in history, Skinner jokes. Kidd's pots of gold are said to dot the whole coast. Gardiner's Island, Cape Cod, and the Florida Keys all claim shares.

Hope of something for nothing drove the digging, Skinner notes. Real wealth was wasted hunting doubloons that never showed. Sea-serpents, stone-throwing devils, and lovers' leaps share the book. V1 warns readers to enjoy the tales without trusting the maps. Skinner's dry humor makes this the most playful volume of his great set.
nan-sherwood-at-rose-ranch-or-the-old-me:
Annie Roe Carr opens this Nan Sherwood tale as school reopens. Early chapters bring new girls and a curfew song. Walking the plank and an unpopular Rhoda stir the school plot. A Mexican girl named Juanita enters the tale.

The treasure of Rose Ranch is named by chapter ten. At last the girls reach the ranch and its open spaces. A round-up and an outlaw close the sample contents. V1 says an old Mexican's hidden gold sets off the hunt. Nan and her friends ride and outwit villains out west, in the bright style series readers loved.
nasa-tm-19650020117-fps-16-radar-jimsphe:
James R Scoggins and Michael Susko, in Marshall's Aero-Astrodynamics Laboratory, reported wind data measured at the Eastern Test Range on July 9, 1965. An FPS-16 radar tracked a Jimsphere, a special balloon made to follow small wind changes faithfully. Launch teams at the range need accurate winds high above the pad.

Radar tracking of such a balloon gives a detailed wind profile. Those profiles help decide whether a launch can proceed safely. They also feed studies of how winds vary with height. Scoggins and Susko present the measured data from the range, in a form other launch and weather workers could use directly.
nasa-tm-19650022493-research-within-the-:
Robert E Bourdeau, of the Space Sciences Division at Goddard, surveyed research within the atmosphere, with stress on the ionosphere. That charged layer was once studied only from the ground. Rockets and satellites could now pass through the region itself. Bourdeau says those chances have greatly enriched understanding of how the ionosphere behaves.

He also credits new ground-based experiments for part of the gain. The ionosphere holds charged particles with very small thermal energies. It forms when sunlight ionizes the neutral air high above Earth. Bourdeau's survey shows a field being remade by direct measurement, a theme across space science at that time.
nasa-tm-19650025671-vacancy-formation-in:
Hubert H Grimes at Lewis Research Center measured tiny defects in gold wire under great pressure for this February 1964 article draft. A vacancy is a missing atom in a crystal, an empty site in the metal's regular pattern. Grimes used changes in electrical resistance in gold wires to count such defects. The wires were held under high hydrostatic pressure, squeezed evenly from all sides.

Defect levels affect how a metal conducts and how it ages. Pressure changes the energy needed to form a vacancy. Measuring that change tests basic theories of metals. The work was prepared for a journal of applied physics, a sign that space agency laboratories also did deep basic research.
nasa-tm-19660020100-some-studies-on-the-:
David A Evensen and Robert E Fulton at Langley presented studies in October 1965 on how thin shell structures answer sudden loads. Shells form rocket tanks, fuselage skins, and nose cones. Their response is nonlinear, meaning it does not grow in simple proportion to the load. Topics in the catalog note include flexural vibration of thin circular cylinders under motion.

Buckling of shallow, conical, and spherical shells under sharp pressure is also treated. A shell that survives steady loads can still collapse under a pulse. Dynamic stability was the theme of the conference they addressed. Their studies gave shell designers test-based guidance for a failure mode that steady analysis cannot predict well.
nasa-tm-19660021037-analysis-of-the-moti:
C R Hayleck Jr at Goddard analyzed how a satellite turns when a reaction wheel does the turning, in this December 1965 report. A reaction wheel is a spinning disk inside the satellite. Speeding or slowing the wheel rotates the craft the other way. Hayleck studies the pair as one assembly, tuned for the least weight and power that can do the job.

His case is a slewing maneuver, a planned turn from one aim point to another. The wheel and the satellite trade motion back and forth during the turn. Sizing the wheel too small makes the turn slow or impossible. Sizing it too large wastes mass and power. The analysis gives designers the trade in usable form.
nasa-tm-19660030132-the-relations-betwee:
Robert A. Bruce, of NASA's Langley Research Center, gave this talk at a training program at Wallops Island, Virginia, in August 1966. The audience was learning bio-space technology. Bruce's theme is the two-way pull between a science experiment and the spacecraft built to carry it.

He walks through the steps that connect what an experiment needs with what a spacecraft can provide. To make the links concrete, the talk uses a made-up biological experiment as its example. Each requirement the experiment sets, such as its environment, then shapes a design choice. The lecture notes preserve that lesson for mission planners.
nasa-tm-19670009442-jupiter-s-magnetosph:
J. A. Gledhill wrote this paper at NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center in February 1967, in its Ionospheric Physics Preprint Series. Gledhill was a senior postdoctoral research associate there. His subject is Jupiter's magnetosphere, the huge bubble of magnetic field around the giant planet. The paper asks what happens to the charged gas trapped inside it.

Jupiter spins fast, completing a full turn roughly every ten hours. If its magnetospheric plasma co-rotates with the planet, centrifugal force flings that plasma outward along the field lines. Near the orbit of the moon Io, the outward force already far exceeds gravity. Gledhill argues there is a maximum plasma density the field can hold in co-rotation at any distance. Beyond it, the plasma breaks away, carrying the field with it. He estimates that maximum density in the equatorial plane by balancing magnetic energy against rotational energy.
nasa-tm-19680018225-transport-properties:
Richard S. Brokaw of Lewis Research Center reviews transport properties of high temperature gases in this 1967 symposium paper. Transport properties include viscosity, diffusion, and thermal conductivity. They govern how gases flow and carry heat in engines and reentry flows.

For cool dilute gases, Chapman-Enskog theory already describes behavior well. Heat conduction is trickier, since rotation and vibration inside molecules add to the heat flux. Work by Mason and Monchick improved that part of the theory, Brokaw notes. At high temperatures, mobile chemical equilibria and free radicals change gas behavior further. Brokaw argues the framework can still predict properties for most practical needs.
nasa-tm-19680024873-an-implantable-multi:
C. M. Winget, J. M. Pope, and colleagues at Ames Research Center describe a tiny radio transmitter built to work inside a living body. Their paper was given at a November 1967 Boston meeting on engineering in medicine and biology. The unit reads four body temperatures at once and sends them out by radio, with no wires through the skin.

Small size and low power use suit the device for long implant tests, the authors note. A ring counter samples a reference resistor and four heat sensors in turn, each shaping the pulse timing of a small oscillator. Such readouts serve studies of daily body rhythms. The animal can be watched closely while nothing outside disturbs it.
nasa-tm-19680025079-the-dry-massive-mode:
Patrick Thaddeus of the Goddard Institute for Space Studies defends a dry, massive model of Venus's atmosphere in this paper. In that model, a deep carbon dioxide atmosphere with no water droplets or dust explains radio observations. Pressure-induced absorption then requires a high ground pressure to fit the data.

Such an atmosphere holds so much heat that nightside cooling stays slight. That creates a problem for the observed microwave phase effect, a small intensity change. Thaddeus argues a model supporter can question whether that effect is real. Measurement errors could fake so small a signal, he notes. He reviews the effect's history at two wavelengths to support the doubt.
nasa-tm-19680025201-the-structure-of-the:
Joseph S. Hogan, of the Goddard Institute for Space Studies and New York University, models the structure of the Martian atmosphere in this study. No spacecraft had yet landed on Mars, so its air had to be built from telescope data and physics. Hogan's model reaches from the surface up into the ionosphere, the charged upper layer observers had detected.

His calculations follow how sunlight is absorbed in carbon dioxide bands and how the gas radiates heat away. A separate chemistry calculation tracks how sunlight breaks carbon dioxide apart and what heating that causes. Weighing mixing against that chemistry, he sets upper and lower limits on particle density in the ionosphere. The scan text is partly garbled, but the model's scope reads clearly.
nasa-tm-19700025450-analysis-of-rendezvo:
Rendezvous radar tracking needs for Mission D are analyzed in this Houston internal note, number MSC-EG-69-6. The radar had to have its angle bias corrected while the two craft flew together. Mission D was Apollo 9, the first crewed flight of the lunar module, tested in Earth orbit.

A data book rule required fifteen minutes of steady radar tracking before any maneuver based on radar updates. The analysis asks whether that much tracking is truly needed to correct the angle bias in the guidance computer. Simulations with only ten minutes of tracking, the summary reports, showed no real fuel penalty. The standing rule, the authors conclude, is a conservative one.
nasa-tm-19700026380-investigation-of-the:
NASA issued this general working paper, number 10,044, on pilot control of gliding parachutes. It investigates what a pilot must see to steer such a parachute well. The goal was landing spacecraft on land rather than at sea, which demanded a far more guided final descent.

The study lays out the mode of operation first, then the test program objectives. Testing ran in three phases, each with its own vehicles and systems described in turn. By comparing phases, the investigators could separate what the pilot saw from what the craft itself did. The aim throughout was a firm list of visual references a pilot needs to land the parachute where intended.
nasa-tm-19710009389-an-evaluation-of-the:
J. W. Montano of NASA's Astronautics Laboratory wrote this evaluation in February 1971, issued as NASA TM X-64569. Its subject is A-286, a stainless alloy strengthened by cold working, meaning it is squeezed or rolled before use to make it harder. Montano set out to measure the alloy's mechanical strength and its resistance to stress corrosion cracking.

The report's contents lay out tensile tests, hardness checks, and low-temperature test work on bar specimens from two makers, Carpenter and Armco. Figures track longitudinal tensile specimens, notched specimens, and hardness across different amounts of cold work. Results and conclusions follow the test sections, giving engineers a compact record of how the worked alloy behaves under load and in cold service.
nasa-tm-19710013626-analysis-of-rotation:
John Zuk and Lawrence P Ludwig of the Lewis Research Center wrote this paper for a May 1971 engineering meeting. It analyzes gas flow across the sealing dam of a noncontacting shaft face seal. Such seals limit leakage along spinning shafts in engines and pumps. Rotation of the seal faces changes the flow in ways simple formulas miss.

The authors treated steady, smooth, subsonic flow at steady temperature. They worked out leakage rates and pressure patterns across the dam. They also gave the conditions where a simpler hydrostatic formula stays valid. The error from using that shortcut is stated. Handy formulas cover leakage, opening force, and the center of pressure.
nasa-tm-19720017690-unipolar-induction-i:
Unipolar Induction in the Magnetosphere presents a new theory of how the solar wind powers Earth's magnetic bubble. Its author names are illegible in the scan. A conductor moving through a magnetic field generates electric currents, an effect called unipolar induction. The paper asks how much of the magnetosphere's activity that effect can explain.

Treating the magnetosheath as a simple ohmic conductor, the theory shows induction can energize several current flows in the magnetosphere. It explains the correlation between the east-west part of the interplanetary magnetic field and polar electric fields and magnetic variations. In the tail region it accounts for effects tied to the field's north-south part. When that field points southward, the theory allows a large energy input into the magnetosphere.
nasa-tm-19720018198-apollo-15-mission-ma:
The Mission Evaluation Team at the Manned Spacecraft Center issued this anomaly report in December 1971. It is report MSC-05805, anomaly report number one for Apollo 15. During the return to Earth, one of the command module's three main parachutes failed. The crew still splashed down safely, but NASA needed the cause. A failed parachute on a crewed flight demands a full investigation.

Investigators studied several possible failure paths in turn. They examined malfunctions in the forward heat shield area. They studied a broken riser, one of the straps tying canopy to capsule. They also studied fuel expelled from the command module's steering thrusters. The catalog record says a most probable cause was identified. The report runs to thirty two pages.
nature-and-human-nature:
Thomas Chandler Haliburton published Nature and Human Nature in 1855. Its first chapter brings back Sam Slick, his famous clockmaker, at a squire's door. Chapter heads promise clippers and steamers, a woman's heart, and a new way to learn Gaelic.

Later heads turn to a day on the lake, a foggy night, and female colleges. Others name gipsying, a betrothal, a honeymoon, and being lost at sea. Haliburton mixes outdoor sport with sharp talk on manners and love. The Pope lines on the title page set the aim: catch manners living as they rise.
news-from-nowhere:
William Morris, poet, craftsman, and socialist, wrote this tale of a dream England in 1890. It first ran in the Commonweal, the journal of his own league. Morris wrote it in part as a reply to Bellamy's Looking Backward of two years past.

A man wakes in a Thames side England where mills, cash, and slums have all passed away. Folk work at crafts they love, share goods in common, and live in a green, clean land. The book is the chief utopian tale of its decade, and a hymn to work done with joy.
no-13-washington-square:
Leroy Scott published No. 13 Washington Square in 1914, a New York tale named for a house address. Chapter one meets the great Mrs De Peyster. An amiable young gentleman enters next, and the lady stands as mistress of her house. A front picture shows a speaker who never suspected ending in such a little blaze.

A slight predicament and the honor of the name trouble the house next. Behind the blinds, the honeymooners, and the flight move the plot along. The Reverend Mr Pyecroft visits, and an attic room holds a secret. Domestic scenes and a happy family close the contents. Scott plays society manners against house mystery.
no-thoroughfare:
Charles Dickens opens No Thoroughfare with an overture, not a chapter. The date is set with care: November the thirtieth, 1835, by the great clock of Saint Paul's. It is ten at night in London. Lesser church clocks strain their metal throats around the cathedral bell.

One clock lags behind the rest, lower and nearer to the ear. It belongs to the Hospital for Foundling Children. Dickens recalls when foundlings were left, no questions asked, in a cradle at the gate. Now mothers must answer inquiries and give up all claim forever. A veiled lady flutters near the hospital gate. Mystery starts with her.
old-saint-paul-s-a-tale-of-the-plague-an:
William Harrison Ainsworth wrote this novel of plague and fire. The preface is dated November 30, 1841. The tale centers on Saint Paul's Cathedral in London. Book one opens in April 1665, plague year. A grocer of Wood Street shuts his family indoors.

on-the-evolution-of-language-first-annua:

over-here: Edgar A. Guest published Over Here in Chicago in 1918. He dedicated the poems To the Mothers Over Here. It is a home-front book for the First World War. paul-and-virginia-from-the-french-of-j-b:

pericles-prince-of-tyre: The hosted sample here shows only the front matter of Pericles, Prince of Tyre, the act and scene list and the start of the persons of the play. No dialogue is visible. pieces-of-eight-being-the-authentic-narr:

poule-noire:
La Poule Noire, The Black Pullet, is a French grimoire framed as the memoir of a Napoleonic officer. The narrator tells of learning talismanic magic in Egypt during the French campaign there. This text, dated about 1820, became the great talismanic grimoire of the French tradition.

Its teaching centers on talismans and rings said to bring riches, love, and protection. Egyptian color dresses older European magic in exotic clothes. The black hen of the title belongs to a rite for finding treasure. Readers loved the mixture of adventure story and working manual. The Black Pullet shows the grimoire changing with its century, adopting Egypt as magic's fashionable homeland.
seneca-letters-lucilius-gummere:
Seneca wrote his 124 Moral Letters to Lucilius near the end of his life, around 65 AD, after retiring from Nero's court. Richard M. Gummere's Loeb translation, made between 1917 and 1925, is the text here. The letters look like private mail; they are really a course in Stoic living.

Nearly every letter handles one knot: time wasted, fear of death, anger, wealth, crowds, or pain. Seneca answers with short drills, sharp examples, and orders to practice daily. He admits his own faults as he writes, which keeps the advice human. The letters are still the warmest guide to Roman Stoicism we have.
sidonia-the-sorceress-the-supposed-destr: Wilhelm Meinhold's eerie German novel — translated by Lady Wilde, Oscar's mother — tells of Sidonia von Bork, accused of witchcraft against the dukes of Pomerania. sir-thomas-more: An Elizabethan play about Henry VIII's great chancellor, Sir Thomas More, including the famous riot scene many scholars credit to Shakespeare's own hand. tales-from-shakespeare: Charles and Mary Lamb's beloved retellings of Shakespeare's plays in plain prose, written for young readers in 1807. the-air-ship-boys-or-the-quest-of-the-az: H. L. Sayler's young aeronauts fly south in their airship seeking the lost treasure of the Aztecs. Ruins, jungles, and rivals await in this high-flying adventure. Written when airships promised the future, it captures all the romance of early aviation.
the-autobiography-of-mark-rutherford-edi: William Hale White’s honest life of Mark Rutherford the dissenter. It is a Victorian spiritual classic, quietly told. Doubt and faith contend in these pages. Honest and deeply moving, a quiet masterpiece, honest and moving.
the-bobbsey-twins-at-the-seashore: Laura Lee Hope takes the Bobbseys to the seashore for sand, surf, and a seaside mystery. Nan, Bert, Freddie, and Flossie enjoy classic summer fun in this sunny series entry. Generations of children spent happy hours with the twins by the sea.
the-city-of-fire: Grace Livingston Hill — the beloved author of inspirational romances — sets this story against a city of fire, where faith is tested and love refined. Her wholesome fiction comforted millions of readers in troubled times. Romance with a Christian heart, warmly told.

the-interdependence-of-literature: The Interdependence of Literature explores how great writings shape one another. The thoughtful lecture traces influence across distant ages and tongues. Books appear as one long and lively conversation. A stimulating essay for every lover of literature.
the-land-of-fire-a-tale-of-adventure: The Land of Fire, a tale of adventure, by Mayne Reid. The fiery land. This book preserves that adventure. Writers of history may cite it later. The paper lasts as a quiet witness. Time has kept the file intact.
the-life-of-st-declan-of-ardmore: The medieval Irish life of Saint Declan, who preached in Ireland before Saint Patrick arrived. the-madonna-of-the-future: Henry James's 1873 story about an American artist in Florence waiting for his masterpiece. Ironic and beautifully written, it is James on the expatriate dream. A classic of his early tales. James's artist waits for a perfection that never comes.
the-man-made-world-or-our-androcentric-c: Gilman’s 1911 book: men built this world for men. Clear, sharp, ahead of its day. A founding text of feminism, still fresh, still fresh today. A founding text of feminism, still fresh today, a pioneering critique.

the-poetical-works-of-oliver-wendell-hol: Before the Curfew collects Holmes' evening poems — quiet reflections on age, memory, and the coming night. the-poor-clare: The Poor Clare, Elizabeth Gaskell's ghost story. The nun's tale. This book preserves that story. Its contents inform the historical record. The library keeps the document safe. Writers of history may cite it later. The paper lasts as a quiet witness.

the-prophet-of-berkeley-square: Robert Hichens's 1901 comic novel about a prophet of Berkeley Square: a young man takes a seer's predictions literally. Witty and whimsical, it was a great success. Delightful Edwardian comedy. Hichens's seer causes chaos with every prediction.
the-ruling-passion-tales-of-nature-and-h: Henry Van Dyke's stories of nature and human character, from fishing camps to foreign lands. the-san-francisco-calamity-by-earthquake: Charles Morris's 1906 instant history of the San Francisco earthquake and fire, rushed out while the ruins still smoked. the-sleuth-of-st-james-s-square: Melville Davisson Post's Sleuth of St. James's Square: Randolph Mason's cunning cases. The great American detective's triumphs, ingenious and fair. Classic early crime fiction. Mason's cunning outwits the law itself, post's detective at his best.
the-snare: The Snare, Rafael Sabatini's novel. Its tale unfolds. This book preserves that historical romance. It retains its place in time. Such papers rarely see the light of day. The file is now open to the public.
the-vampyre:

Lord Ruthven is cold, proud, and fair, and he feeds on the lives of those who trust him. A young man who roams with him learns his secret and is bound by an oath not to tell. The tale is the first of the vampire lord in English books, a form that rules to this day.

varney-the-vampyre:

wildfire: A Zane Grey Western about a wild horse named Wildfire and the men who chase him. Swift, romantic, and full of desert color, it is Grey in his element. Classic Western adventure. Grey's wild horses run through some of his finest descriptive writing.
